title: Internal links that sound like a person
metaTitle: Internal links that sound like a person
excerpt: Link from a sentence that says why the next piece helps. A few honest links beat a related-posts block and a trail of read-more.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads, objects set apart so each one stays legible.

faqs.question: How many internal links should a page have?
faqs.answer: As many as you can explain in a sentence, which on a studio essay is usually a few. One should point at the next decision. One may point at the offer, if it fits. A block of related posts at the bottom does not count as explanation, and adding more links does not make the page more helpful.

faqs.question: What should the anchor text say?
faqs.answer: It should say what the reader will get, in the same voice as the sentence. Name the decision or the artifact. Avoid 'click here,' 'read more,' and a stuffed phrase that exists only for a crawler. If the anchor could be dropped onto any paragraph on the site, it is too generic.

faqs.question: Do internal links help search?
faqs.answer: They help a person move to the next useful page, which is the part you can control. Google's title guidance also notes that anchor text is one of the sources used when a title link is generated, so dishonest anchors can confuse that system as well as the reader. Write the anchor for the reader.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Natural internal linking means the link sits inside a sentence that says why the next piece helps. It does not mean a "read more" glued to every paragraph, and it does not mean a block of related posts that could have been generated from tags. A few honest links beat both.

The reader is a founder with another tab open. They will follow a reason. They will not follow a hint that you were told to add links.

## A sentence that names the next job

Write the link at the moment the next question appears. You have explained that a meta description should state an outcome. The next question is whether more than one URL is allowed to wear that sentence. That is a reason to link, and the sentence can carry it without a special format. "Once the sentence is right, only one URL should wear it" is already almost the link. Put the anchor on the words that name the destination's job.

If you cannot finish the sentence without the phrase "check out this article," you do not have a reason yet. Leave the link out. A page with two earned links is healthier than a page with fifteen obligatory ones. Orphans worry people who look at crawl maps. Readers do not feel orphaned. They feel interrupted.

Place most of these links after the answer, not before it. A stranger should get the point of this page before they are invited elsewhere. A link in the first screen that skips to another essay is how a careful piece becomes a hallway. Hallways are for sites that do not trust any single room. Trust the room. Offer the door when the reader has what they came for and the next decision is real.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether someone can leave having learned enough, and whether the page is something you would recommend to a friend. A link is a recommendation. You would not recommend a friend twelve things in one breath. You would say, "this is the part you need next." Write that way. The guidance also treats clear, descriptive headings as a sign of care. Anchors are small headings in the middle of a paragraph. Vague ones fail the same test.

## Why "read more" fails

"Read more" says nothing about the destination. It could be a footnote, a product, or a confession. The reader has to leave the sentence, visit, and come back if they guessed wrong. On a phone, coming back is how you lose them. The cost of a vague anchor is a broken paragraph and a wasted visit.

The same failure hides in polite variants. "Learn more." "Discover how." "See our thoughts." These are throat-clearing. They show that the writer knew a link was required and did not know what it was for. Delete the link until you know. A studio that sounds specific in the prose and generic in the anchors has a seam, and founders notice seams more than they notice the absence of a link.

There is a searchable version of this mistake. The anchor is a keyword you wish the target to rank for, jammed beside a sentence it does not continue. The paragraph was about a salesperson between calls. The anchor says "best CRM software for small business growth." Nobody in the paragraph was speaking that way. The link is a billboard nailed to a conversation. Take it down.

[Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) notes that the anchor text on your pages, and the text of links that point at a page, are among the sources used to build a title in search. That is a practical reason to be honest, beyond manners. If every link to a piece says something the piece is not, you are feeding a confused title. If the anchors match the visible heading and the actual point, you are being consistent. You still write the anchor for the human who has to click it. The consistency is a side effect of that, not a puzzle to game.

## A few links, chosen

On a typical studio essay, a handful is plenty.

1. The next decision, linked in a sentence that says why it is next.
2. One offer, only if this page earned it: the work, the services, or a call.
3. A definition or a standard, when you relied on it, linked at the claim.

That list is a ceiling more often than a floor. Some pages need one link. A short repair note might only point at the current how-to. Forcing a second link to "keep the cluster healthy" is how clusters start to sound like directories.

Vary the destination according to the reader's job. A page about reading a portfolio should send people to the work. A page about scoping should send them to what to prepare, not to every other scoping synonym you published. Look at Hanabi's public projects only when the link is about that kind of work. Down the Cove belongs near an ecommerce migration point. Got Next, Leadly, or Trade Moai belong near a point about product UI. Thomas Bewick belongs near editorial craft. Dropping all of them into every essay as proof of life is a logo wall in sentence form.

Do not link the same destination twice with two anchors because you were afraid the first one would be missed. Repetition reads as anxiety. If the first sentence was clear, trust it.

## Anchors that sound like the paragraph

The anchor can be a few words. It does not have to be the full title of the target, and it should not be a URL printed in the sentence. "Canonical URLs for a studio site" is a fine anchor if the sentence is formal. "Only one official URL" is better if that is the point you are making. Match the diction you already used. A casual paragraph that suddenly links "utilize our comprehensive canonicalization framework" has been captured by another genre.

Keep the anchor inside the grammar. The sentence should still parse if the link styling disappeared. "Read the next piece, which explains permissions," works. "Permissions" as a naked link after a period does not. Fragments are how a generated block behaves. You are not a generated block.

Avoid anchors that promise a result the target does not deliver. If the next page is a method, do not anchor "the guaranteed fix." If the next page is a limit, say the limit. Overselling an internal link is the same trust leak as overselling a title. The reader clicks, feels handled, and discounts the next recommendation. You get very few of those before the session becomes a skim.

## Where links belong on a studio site

Navigation is a set of links, and it should stay boring. Work, writing, a way to talk. Do not stuff the menu with every spoke in a cluster. The menu is for the rooms. In-sentence links are for the doors between answers.

The footer can carry a small number of durable pages: the studio, the feed, a way to contact. It should not be a second index of every post, updated by a widget. Widgets feel like furniture. People walk around them.

Inside a post, a single aside is enough if you have one genuine branch. "If you are maintaining the old page rather than writing a new one, the update habit is different." That is a branch. Five asides are a maze. Pick the branch the majority of your readers are on, and let the others use the index.

Project pages should link to the relevant writing only when the writing explains a decision visible in the project. A case study that ends with six unrelated essays looks unsure of its own story. The story is the project. The essay is optional depth.

From the blog back to the work, use the same restraint. One path. The reader who wants everything can open the index. The reader who wants the next step should be given one, not a buffet.

## What a related-posts block gets wrong

A block of cards at the bottom, titled "Related," chosen by shared tags, fails in a specific way. It does not say why. The cards repeat titles the reader has not been prepared for. The images, if they are quiet heroes, do not explain the relationship either. The block is a confession that the body of the article never found a moment to recommend anything.

If you keep a block, make it manual and short, and put a reason on each line. Two items. A clause each. The moment you automate it, the reasons disappear and the city-swap problem returns: everything tagged "design" is related to everything else tagged "design." That is true and useless.

Do not duplicate the block with the same items in the sidebar. Repetition of a weak recommendation does not turn it into a strong one. It trains the eye to skip the region. Then, when you finally write a real sentence-link, the reader may skip that too, because you taught them that links on this site are furniture.

Review the block the way you review a paragraph. Read it aloud. If you would be embarrassed to say "related: ten titles" at the end of a talk, do not make the page say it.

## The path a founder walks

Imagine one founder, not a segment. She read the page on descriptions because the search result was specific. She needs the next constraint, which is the official URL. She does not need, yet, the essay on CRM settings. Later, if she is building a product, she will. The link you offer today should be the one she needs today.

Walk that path yourself once a month. Start at a post that earns conversations. Follow only the in-sentence links. See where you are after three clicks. You should be either deeper into the decision or at the offer. If you are on a random tag, the links are not a path. If you are on the same page via a logo that is somehow in the prose, the template is interrupting.

Fix the path before you add pages. New pages without a sentence to hang them on will be linked from the related block and nowhere else, which is the same as unpublished, except a crawler can find them and a person cannot.

The same habit shows up inside a product, where the "link" is the next control a person needs. [The first screen of a CRM](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-crm) is the next piece, because a salesperson updating a record between calls deserves one obvious object and one action, not a tour and not a pile of related modules.

When the path on the marketing site is ready to be built, not just described, [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover that design and engineering, including the pages and the links between them.
